Characteristic motion and closed-set barriers

A supporting covector records a direction in which a closed set ends. This local information controls two kinds of motion. A Hamiltonian vanishing on every supporting covector transports the covectors themselves. A locally Lipschitz vector field that never points outward transports points of the closed set forward inside it. We prove both assertions, including a single supporting function along a characteristic arc and the distance estimate needed when a nearest point is not unique.

The preceding lesson Both analytic directions at support boundaries, §1 and its support-geometry reading, supplies strict quadratic supporting functions and nearest-point normals. We use the complete smooth inverse and implicit maps, §§16.4–16.5, and smooth parameter flows, §§17.1–17.5. Their finite-dimensional compactness, differentiation and integration inputs are supplied by the calculus foundation, §§12–13, and finite algebra, §§10.1–10.6. No global completeness of a vector field is assumed.

We first specify the ODE input at this regularity. For a locally Lipschitz , choose a closed ball near a fixed point on which and . Such a ball exists by the local definition, shrinking to obtain . For initial data in a smaller concentric ball and sufficiently small , the map

Iteration has a geometric bound on successive differences and converges uniformly to a unique fixed point. Continuity of and the fundamental theorem make it a solution. Two solutions with the same value agree on a short interval by the same contraction estimate; their agreement then extends over the connected common interval by the open-and-closed argument. 6. Exercises with complete solutions

Exercise 1 (a characteristic support arc). Determine the exterior normals of and the Hamilton motion of . Construct (16) through with initial covector .

Solution. Interior points have no normals: a differentiable function at a local maximum on an open ball has zero differential. At a boundary point , both tangent directions are realized by curves in , forcing the differential to be a multiple of . The inward curve makes that multiple nonnegative, hence positive for a nonzero covector. Conversely witnesses every . With , Hamilton's equations are . Direct differentiation of the rotation matrix gives , the unique orbit. The function has differential , vanishes on the circle, and is negative inside. Locally along a short arc these are exactly (16). Also , and vanishes at every normal.

Exercise 3 (the test at a corner). Describe the normals to , express (8) in components, and decide whether preserves forward.

Solution. In the relative interior of the face , two-sided variation forces , and inward variation forces . All nonzero such covectors are witnessed by a linear function. The other face is analogous. At the corner both components must be nonpositive, and every nonzero such covector is again witnessed linearly. Interior points have no normals. Thus the test is and on the respective faces, including both conditions at the corner. The proposed field fails the second condition for . Its solution from is , which leaves immediately.

Exercise 4 (the Lipschitz assumption matters). Show that passes the normal test for , yet has a trajectory leaving . Contrast .

Solution. Normals occur only at zero with . Both fields vanish there, so (8) holds. For the square-root field , is a solution from zero and leaves . The field is not locally Lipschitz at zero, since . The positive-part field is Lipschitz with constant one, as checking two arguments of the same or opposite signs proves . Theorem 2 applies. From , its constant solution is unique by contraction. For positive initial data , attaining equality in (11).

Solution. Convention (12) gives . Corollary 5 would force , a contradiction. No smooth-manifold structure of the full normal set was presumed.

Exercise 6 (sharp dimension bounds). For , exhibit vanishing functions with independent differentials at its normals, and with independent fiber gradients. Include .

Solution. The tangent and inward tests give exactly the normals , . The functions vanish there with independent differentials. The first have independent fiber gradients; the last has zero fiber gradient. Both bounds are sharp. For , still has a nonzero full differential, but no nonempty independent list of fiber gradients is possible: vanishing on the whole positive normal ray forces the fiber derivative to vanish there.

Exercise 7 (why base velocity is required). For and , verify normal preservation and explain why a fixed cannot satisfy on a nontrivial time interval.

Solution. Every nonzero covector at zero is a normal, witnessed by , and these are all normals. The Hamiltonian vanishes there; its flow is , restricted so . It remains in the actual normal set. But a fixed function has just one derivative at zero, which cannot equal the varying . Here , the excluded case for (16).

Exercise 8 (translation of an initial graph). For , with constant , compute Lemma 3's solution for arbitrary smooth . If on , prove that every translation segment from which lies in lies in .

Solution. The orbit is . The action integrand is , giving and . Differentiation verifies (13). For the closed set, gives the inequalities for both and . Theorem 2 gives invariance on the actual connected existence interval of this trajectory. Thus every segment from staying in stays in ; no extension across a missing part of the domain is asserted.

In dimension zero the punctured cotangent space is empty, every trajectory is constant, and the normal and Hamilton statements with a marked nonzero covector have no instance.
